Kenapa Harus Pakai Bitcoin? Menurut Iran, sistem ini dipakai untuk: • Menghindari sanksi internasional • Menggunakan jalur pembayaran di luar sistem keuangan AS • Meminimalkan risiko transaksi diblokir/disita Kalo diibaratkan seorang pemain catur, Iran seperti Grand Master yang mampu untuk memikirkan berbagai aspek sebelum melangkahkan bidak caturnya...

With the war in the Middle East pushing oil prices up, things are getting harder everywhere. Unsubsidised RON95 in Malaysia just hit RM3.87 a litre. Our neighbours are under real pressure. Philippines. Thailand. Cambodia. Laos. Even Australia is facing a fuel crisis right now. These are not just statistics. These are real people, families trying to get to work, small business owners watching their costs double overnight, ordinary folks doing their best in a situation they didn’t create. If you’re reading this, hang in there. But yesterday, our PM announced that our subsidised petrol at RM1.99 stays. Yes, the quota drops from 300L to 200L in April. And I keep thinking, this kind of stability doesn’t just happen. It took decades. Generations of leaders building diplomatic relationships quietly in the background. Policy makers running the numbers at midnight. Civil servants holding things together without anyone knowing their name. People who never made the news but made the difference. This moment of relative calm, they built it. Long before this crisis ever came. But it also took something very Malaysian. We have this rare ability to sit with anyone, different races, different religions, different backgrounds and just get along. In a world that’s fracturing right now, that’s actually a superpower. clean_text: No and here's my reasoning : Gold trades at the exact same price worldwide - whether in Malaysia, the US, Europe, or anywhere. Silver, platinum, copper, crude oil, and other global commodities are priced uniformly too. A gram of gold doesn’t get cheaper just because the local cost of living is lower. So why is human labor treated so differently? A waitress doing the exact same work (10-hour shifts, 6 days a week, serving tables, carrying trays, handling customers) earns a tiny fraction in a developing country compared to the same job in a first-world nation. We’re told it’s okay because “cost of living is lower” and “productivity differs.” Nonsense! Equal work deserves equal pay, no matter where you are on Earth. Look at the blatant hypocrisy: Expat General Managers and top executives in the same hotels and restaurants get paid international rates - often similar (or more) to what they’d earn back home, plus expat allowances, hardship allowance, housing, flights, and bonuses. Their salaries are globally equitable. But the local staff doing the real daily work get exploited with local poverty wages. Why? Multinational companies happily charge the same (or even higher) prices for their products and services in poor countries, but refuse to pay fair global wages to the people who make the business run. Are human beings worth less than bars of gold or barrels of oil? Human lives and effort should have one standard of dignity worldwide. Paying people less simply because they were born in a poorer country is pure exploitation dressed up as “market reality.” It’s time to end this double standard. Equal work = equal pay globally. Anything less devalues human life based on geography. The world can afford fairness but it just refuses to prioritize people over profit.

Mobility remains a high frequency engagement engine that feeds the SuperApp flywheel into deliveries, ads, and fintech. Deliveries (food + growing grocery/quick commerce) is the largest revenue segment but lower margin; however, GrabFin with explosive Atome Frequency business model, advertising, GrabUnlimited, and operational efficiency are the paths to grow higher margins there. SEA will remain price sensitive for a long time, at least for the next 5-10 years. The real money is in Financial Services, Ads, Subscription, Quick-Commerce(For vol), B2B solutions, and Tourism(higher margin services). 2. Why driver/courier density is critical for quick-commerce! Quick-commerce (GrabMart, grocery, essentials, and similar on demand logistics) is highly sensitive to speed and reliability. Customers expect short delivery windows. That only works with dense local supply of drivers/couriers who are already active nearby. Many are willing to pay a premium for shorter time deliveries. Thin supply means longer wait times, higher failed deliveries, more incentives needed to pull partners into the right zones, and ultimately weaker demand. Dense supply improves utilisation, allows better batching and matching, and makes the service feel reliable enough for habitual use. Grab has repeatedly treated partner supply as a foundational marketplace health metric for both Mobility and Deliveries for this reason. Demand side: Competitive (or deliberately affordable) consumer pricing drives volume and habit. Once someone opens the app regularly for rides or food, the marginal cost of acquiring them for grocery/quick-commerce drops sharply because the user is already inside the ecosystem. Cross selling inside the SuperApp is far cheaper than external paid acquisition. Supply side: Better partner economics (as in the Malaysia package) keep the network dense without constantly burning cash on incentives. Unit economics: A modest positive contribution margin (or even near-breakeven on the pure transaction after incentives) can still be excellent strategy if it compounds the network. Scale brings operating leverage, better matching efficiency, and the ability to layer higher margin revenue (advertising to merchants, promotions, financial services, subscriptions) on top of the same transactions without raising base consumer prices much. The SuperApp effect: more users → more demand → more drivers → better service → more users) do the acquisition work once density is reached. Mobility remains useful here as a high frequency traffic engine that feeds the rest of the app. 3. clean_text: Mahathir Mohamad has been using this narrative for decades: that Malays are perpetually under threat, and only Malay political unity can “save” the country. But the reality in 2026 is far more complicated — and far less dramatic — than the apocalyptic picture he paints. Malaysia is not “slipping from Malay hands.” Malays still dominate every major pillar of state power: the civil service, police, military, monarchy, Islamic institutions, and the vast majority of political leadership. The Prime Minister himself is Malay. To suggest Malays are on the verge of extinction politically is simply not grounded in reality. What has actually failed is not “Malay unity” — but the old politics of fear. For years, leaders across the political spectrum sold the idea that Malays must unite against non-Malays, liberals, secularists, DAP, the West, or whoever the enemy of the week was. But younger Malaysians increasingly care about governance, corruption, wages, education, healthcare, and cost of living — not endless racial paranoia. Ironically, Mahathir himself helped create the political culture he now laments. During his long years in power, UMNO-era patronage politics enriched elites while many ordinary Malays remained economically insecure. Huge scandals, cronyism, weakened institutions, and race-based dependency politics did not strengthen the Malays in the long run — they weakened public trust. His statement also reveals a troubling mindset: that the country belongs to one race. Malaysia does not “belong” exclusively to Malays, Chinese, Indians, Orang Asli, Sabahans, or Sarawakians. It belongs to all citizens. The Constitution already protects Malay special position, Islam, the monarchy, and Bahasa Melayu. Those safeguards are not disappearing tomorrow because Malays are politically divided. The bigger danger to Malaysia is not the lack of Malay unity. It is the constant weaponisation of ethnic fear to protect political relevance. A mature nation cannot keep functioning on existential panic every election cycle. If Malay politics keeps revolving around “we are under siege,” instead of fixing corruption, education, productivity, brain drain, and institutional decay, then the community risks becoming trapped in permanent insecurity despite holding immense political power. Mahathir’s statement sounds less like a national warning and more like the frustration of an old political era losing its grip on public imagination.

clean_text: It takes courage & strong political will to be different in a world of yes-men & populist politics if we want real, sustainable change. In a world of limited resources, Malaysia has been stretched to its limits on all fronts, including national debt. How much more can the Malaysian government stretch itself beyond its means? When a country has been mismanaged for so long, paying subsidies for subsidy’s sake is not the answer. A well-managed Malaysia should have lower personal income tax, a reasonably attractive corporate tax comparable with our closest neighbours, & a more affordable cost of living for the rakyat—without compromising quality of life—while providing good, accessible healthcare & education for every child. Some estimate that Petronas has paid the government close to RM700 billion (approximately RM685 billion as of end-2025) in dividends since 1974. (Though exact cumulative figures are not published in a continuous official series in recent Petronas integrated reports, which emphasise broader contributions of dividends, taxes, cash/royalty payments & National Trust Fund contributions, the amount paid may exceed RM1.5 trillion by around 2024.) Had our government managed these dividends well, as Norway did & without corruption, Malaysia could be a very wealthy country, maybe even better than Singapore. (Norway converted temporary oil wealth into permanent financial capital under strict rules; Malaysia largely treated Petronas revenues as current budget income, leaving only a small intergenerational fund.) What our government has done with those estimates of “sovereign wealth” from Petronas (between RM700 billion to RM1.5 trillion) should be examined carefully so we can learn from past mistakes. Sovereign wealth should be treated as intergenerational capital rather than wasted, as it has been in Malaysia for five decades. With national debt at a staggering RM1.5 trillion, plus Petronas dividends / payouts estimated at between RM700 billion to RM1.5 trillion, almost RM3 trillion has possibly been lost due to poor governance, corruption & mismanagement over the past 5 decades. Unless we have a party like #Bersama willing to take a tough stand, make unpopular but necessary decisions & call “a spade a spade”, real reform cannot happen. Malaysia will not recover & will continue to spiral under choking national debt & unfettered or undeterred corruption. For real change—political, economic and social—tough decisions are needed to reduce national debt over 5 to 15 or 20 years (three to four PRUs), better manage sovereign wealth for intergenerational wellbeing, improve the quality & relevance of basic and higher education to industry needs, strengthen accessible & affordable healthcare for an ageing population, and reduce economic sectors’ dependence on foreign workers (riddled with corruption & malpractice since the early 1990s because of its lucrativeness) and etc! Another necessary but unpopular step is to reduce drug abuse. Recent news of drug trafficking shows major concerns on enforcement & the extend of weak checkpoints! So many people and families have been destroyed by drugs abuse!
